# Data Types and Their Structure {#sec-data-types}

A table, a sentence, a photograph and a recording are all arrays of numbers by the time a model
sees them. They are not the same kind of array. Each data type has structure the numbers alone
do not announce: order, neighborhoods, frequencies, symmetries. A representation either exposes
that structure to the model or leaves the model to discover it. And an evaluation either
respects it or quietly breaks it. This chapter takes the data types one at a time, then
demonstrates both effects: one on the representation lever, one on evaluation.

## The problem

For each data type, three questions decide what preprocessing makes sense:

1. **What structure is there?** Order in time, adjacency in space, a vocabulary with very
   unequal frequencies, categories without order.
2. **Which invariances are plausible?** A transformation of the input that should not change
   the target. Plausible is not the same as true: an invariance is an assumption about $p$, and
   [Augmentation](09-augmentation.qmd#sec-augmentation) is where assuming it wrongly does harm.
3. **Which representation exposes the structure?** The one under which the target becomes a
   simple function of the features, for the model at hand.

## Assumptions

1. **The structure is a property of $p$, not of the file format.** Rows of a table can be
   ordered in time even when nothing in the table says so.
2. **The model cannot build every representation itself.** A linear model on raw samples
   cannot compute a spectrum; whether a flexible model learns an equivalent transform depends
   on its architecture and data, which is outside this book
   ([transformer-atlas](https://github.com/ioannisantoniadis/transformer-atlas) covers
   architectures).
3. **Evaluation mimics deployment.** Validation examples must relate to training examples the
   way future examples will. If deployment predicts later times, validation must too.

## Derivation or demonstration

**Tabular data.** Columns are numeric (counts, measurements, money), categorical (no order),
ordinal (ordered categories), or dates and times (which carry order, and often cycles). The
structure is in the columns' scales and in which encodings respect them: an ordinal code
asserts an order and equal spacing that a categorical column does not have
([Encoding and Features](07-encoding-and-features.qmd#sec-encoding)). Rows are usually treated
as exchangeable. When they are ordered in time they are not, which is the leakage below.

**Text.** Text is a sequence of tokens from a vocabulary. Word frequencies "approximately
[follow] a simple mathematical form known as Zipf's law", frequency falling roughly as a power
of rank, with "considerable structure" beyond that fit [@piantadosi2014zipf]. Two consequences
recur in this book. A few tokens dominate every count, and most of the vocabulary is rare,
which is the long tail of [Why Power Laws](13-why-power-laws.qmd#sec-long-tail). The Markov
text testbed (T4) builds both properties in exactly. Tokenizer internals are out of scope; no
sibling book covers them.

**Images.** An image is a grid of pixel intensities, where neighboring pixels are related.
Plausible invariances (a small shift, a change of brightness) are assumptions about the task,
not facts about images: a horizontal flip preserves "cat" and destroys "the letter b". T5
includes a synthetic image label whose invariance under an up–down flip, and reversal under a
left–right flip, are exact, for the augmentation experiments.

**Audio and the spectrogram.** A recording is a waveform sampled at a fixed rate. Frequencies
above half the sampling rate cannot be told apart from lower ones. At 8 kHz, the samples of a
5 kHz sine are exactly those of a 3 kHz sine with the sign flipped, since
$\sin(2\pi \cdot 5n/8) = \sin(2\pi n - 2\pi \cdot 3n/8) = -\sin(2\pi \cdot 3n/8)$
(`tests/test_data_types.py::test_aliasing_is_exact_above_half_the_sampling_rate`). Whatever was
above half the rate is folded in before any model sees it.

What distinguishes sounds is usually which frequencies are present, and when. The waveform
encodes that only through oscillations whose phase is arbitrary. The **spectrogram**, the
magnitude of a short-time Fourier transform, measures the energy in each frequency band within
each short window and discards the phase.

{{< include ../includes/cards/spectrogram.md >}}

T5 makes the difference concrete. Two classes of noisy tones, 400–600 Hz and 1,200–1,400 Hz,
each with a random phase, a quarter second at 8 kHz. Across 400 training and 400 test signals
and five seeds, the same regularized logistic regression scores:

- **on the raw waveform:** a test accuracy of 0.49 to 0.53, chance. With a random phase, the
  waveform's distribution is symmetric about zero in both classes, so a linear score cannot
  separate them and does little better than guessing.
- **on the log power spectrum** (the time-averaged spectrogram): 1.00 in every seed.

The model did not change; the representation did
(`tests/test_data_types.py::test_spectrogram_representation_makes_tone_classes_linearly_separable`).

**Time series.** Observations ordered in time are usually autocorrelated: today resembles
yesterday. Leakage, in the sense of Kaufman et al., is "the introduction of information about
the data mining target, which should not be legitimately available to mine from"
[@kaufman2011leakage]. In time, legitimacy has a simple form, which they call a
"no-time-machine requirement": a model may use only what was known before the moment of
prediction. Shuffled cross-validation breaks it. Every validation point has training points
from just before and just after it.

On T5's autocorrelated series (a latent AR(1) with coefficient 0.99, plus noise), a
5-nearest-neighbor regressor on the time index was trained on 2,000 steps and evaluated in three
ways, over ten seeds:

- shuffled 5-fold cross-validation reported a mean squared error of 1.25;
- time-ordered splits reported 59.5;
- the actual error on the next 300 steps averaged 64.3.

Shuffling understated the error by a factor of at least 14 in every seed
(`tests/test_data_types.py::test_shuffled_cross_validation_leaks_time`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: structure in the data constrains both representation and evaluation"}
A representation that makes the target a simple function of the features can turn a task from
impossible to trivial for the same model. An evaluation that breaks the data's ordering
measures interpolation instead of prediction. On an autocorrelated series that can understate
the error by an order of magnitude or more.
:::

{{< include ../includes/cards/time-ordered-split.md >}}

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
`scipy.signal.stft` computes the short-time Fourier transform. Its default window in SciPy 1.18
is `'hann_periodic'`, so pass `window`, `nperseg` and `noverlap` explicitly. scikit-learn's
`TimeSeriesSplit` "returns the first k folds as the train set and the (k+1)-th fold as the test
set", and `KFold` does not shuffle unless `shuffle=True` (scikit-learn 1.9 docstrings).
:::

**Graphs.** Nodes connected by edges, where an example's neighbors carry information about it.
Graph representations are covered in
[modern-ai-systems-and-methods](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/modern-ai-systems-and-methods/chapters/09-graph-neural-networks.html);
the leakage lesson transfers, since a node's neighbors in a validation set may sit in the
training set.

## What it does to the learned model

A representation sets which functions are simple. The spectrogram did not add information to
the tones; it moved the information into a form a linear model can read. The same move recurs
in [Changing the Shape](06-changing-the-shape.qmd#sec-shape) and
[Encoding and Features](07-encoding-and-features.qmd#sec-encoding).

An evaluation split changes nothing about the model and everything about what we believe of
it. The nearest-neighbor model was the same in all three columns of the comparison; only the
estimate of its error moved.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: spectrogram of noisy audio that plays 500 Hz until 0.4 s and 2,000 Hz after; the energy sits on the generating frequencies and switches at the switch time. Panel B: test accuracy of the same logistic regression on raw waveforms and on log power spectra of two classes of noisy tones with random phase (bars: means; dots: 5 seeds). Panel C: for an autocorrelated series, the error a nearest-neighbor model reports under shuffled and time-ordered cross-validation, and its actual error on the next 300 steps (10 seeds; bars are means). The representation decides what a linear model can see; shuffling a time series lets the model look up the answer.](../images/data_types.png){#fig-data-types}

@fig-data-types shows the three effects. Failures that follow from them:

- **A spectrogram with the wrong window.** A short window cannot resolve close frequencies; a
  long one smears changes in time.
- **Leakage that survives a time-ordered split.** Features computed over the whole series
  (a normalizer, a rolling average centered on each point) carry the future into the past.
  This is the leaking-features case of Kaufman et al.
- **A noisy future window.** In the demonstration the time-ordered estimate matched the future
  error on average. Any one 300-step future window, though, varied by nearly a factor of ten
  across seeds (18.6 to 176.6).

## What the toy cannot show

The tones differ in one obvious feature and the series has one source of dependence. Real
audio needs perceptual frequency scales and longer context. Real time series mix trends,
seasonality and changes in regime. Both demonstrations show the direction and the mechanism of
an effect, not its size on real data.
